title: Swedish work culture: fika, lagom and consensus
goal: Take part in a Swedish meeting, agree and disagree the way Swedes do, take feedback gracefully, and pitch a work email at the right level.
bekal: you can agree, disagree softly and help a group reach a decision together
you can make requests and suggestions sound polite with *skulle*, *kunde*, *tänkte* and *vore*
you can open and close a work email correctly for a colleague, a client or an authority
wave: Go back to Unit 15 (Reported speech II): report five lines from the meeting in this unit with reporting verbs: *Mattias tyckte att…*, *Leila påpekade att…*, *Karin frågade om…*. Watch the tense shift and BIFF.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Veckomötet
dialogs.intro: Monday afternoon, the weekly team meeting. On the agenda: which part of the client's app the team should build first. Karin is chairing, and there are coffee and cinnamon buns on the table, of course.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Då kör vi igång. Första punkten: vad ska vi prioritera i appen?
lines.id: Right, let's get going. First item: what should we prioritize in the app?
lines.literal: then drive we going. first point-the: what shall we prioritize in app-the?

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Jag tycker att vi ska börja med inloggningen. Utan den funkar ingenting.
lines.id: I think we should start with the login. Without it, nothing works.
lines.literal: I think that we shall begin with login-the. without it works nothing.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Bra poäng. Samtidigt ser jag det lite annorlunda. Kunden pratade mest om bokningen.
lines.id: Good point. At the same time, I see it a little differently. The client talked mostly about booking.
lines.literal: good point. same-time see I it little differently. customer-the talked most about booking-the.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Dian, du var ju med på kundmötet. Vad tycker du?
lines.id: Dian, you were at the client meeting. What do you think?
lines.literal: Dian, you were as-you-know with at customer-meeting-the. what think you?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag håller med Leila, faktiskt. De nämnde bokningen minst fem gånger.
lines.id: I agree with Leila, actually. They mentioned booking at least five times.
lines.literal: I hold with Leila, actually. they mentioned booking-the least five times.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Okej, det visste jag inte. Då kunde vi kanske göra en enkel inloggning först?
lines.id: OK, I didn't know that. Then maybe we could do a simple login first?
lines.literal: okay, that knew I not. then could we maybe do a simple login first?

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Och lägga mest tid på bokningen. Det kan jag leva med.
lines.id: And spend most of the time on booking. I can live with that.
lines.literal: and lay most time on booking-the. that can I live with.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Låter bra. Kan alla ställa sig bakom det?
lines.id: Sounds good. Can everyone get behind that?
lines.literal: sounds good. can all place themselves behind it?

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Absolut. Det känns som en bra kompromiss.
lines.id: Absolutely. It feels like a good compromise.
lines.literal: absolutely. it feels like a good compromise.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Då är vi överens. Jag skickar ut ett kort protokoll efter mötet.
lines.id: Then we're agreed. I'll send out short minutes after the meeting.
lines.literal: then are we agreed. I send out a short protocol after meeting-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ska vi inte rösta först?
lines.id: Shouldn't we vote first?
lines.literal: shall we not vote first?

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Rösta? Nej då, vi har ju redan landat i ett beslut tillsammans.
lines.id: Vote? Oh no, we've already landed on a decision together.
lines.literal: vote? no then, we have as-you-know already landed in a decision together.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Välkommen till svensk möteskultur, Dian. Vi pratar tills alla är nöjda.
lines.id: Welcome to Swedish meeting culture, Dian. We talk until everyone's happy.
lines.literal: welcome to Swedish meeting-culture, Dian. we talk until all are pleased.

notes: **Då kör vi igång** — the standard way to open a meeting: "Right, let's get going." *Köra igång* (literally "drive going") means to start something up. *Första punkten* is the first item on *dagordningen* (the agenda), pronounced **DAHG-ood-ning-en**.

**Bra poäng. Samtidigt ser jag det lite annorlunda.** — this is the textbook Swedish way to disagree: acknowledge first, then disagree with a softener (*lite*, *kanske*, *samtidigt*). A flat *Du har fel* (You're wrong) is rarely heard in a Swedish meeting room and would sound almost rude.

**Jag håller med Leila** — *hålla med* (to agree) is a particle verb, so *med* carries the stress: **HOL-lah MEH**. You agree **with** a person (*hålla med någon*) and **about** a thing (*hålla med om något*): *Jag håller med om det.*

**Då kunde vi kanske göra…** — Mattias uses the past form *kunde* (could) and *kanske* (maybe) to turn a proposal into an invitation. The past tense as a softener is one of the most useful tools at B1; see the grammar box.

**Kan alla ställa sig bakom det?** — literally "Can everyone place themselves behind it?": the chair's question before closing an item. **Överens** (agreed) is stressed at the end: **ö-ver-ENS**. *Vi är överens* = We agree, it's settled.

**Ska vi inte rösta?** — in many cultures a vote is the fair way to decide. In a Swedish team it can feel almost confrontational, because someone has to lose. Decisions are *förankrade* (anchored): talked through, often in the corridor and at *fika*, until everyone can live with them.

grammars.title: Agreeing and disagreeing the Swedish way
body: Swedish meetings run on consensus, and the language reflects it. Notice how many of the phrases below contain a softener: *lite*, *kanske*, *helt*, *ett steg till*.

head: Function
Svenska
English
rows: Jag förstår hur du tänker, men…
I see what you mean, but…
I see it a bit differently.
Jag är inte helt säker på det.
I'm not entirely sure about that.
Då är vi överens. / Då landar vi där.
Then we're agreed. / Let's settle on that.

after: *Tänk om* + a past form makes a gentle proposal: *Tänk om vi började med bokningen?* (What if we started with booking?) The past tense here does not refer to the past; it makes the idea sound open, as in English "What if we started…".

grammars.title: Softening with the past tense
body: Like English *could*, *would* and *I was wondering*, Swedish uses past forms to make requests and suggestions sound less pushy. At work this is close to obligatory: the present tense can sound like an order.

head: Direct
Softer
rows: Det är bra om du kommer.

after: **Vore** is the old subjunctive of *vara*, which you met with unreal conditions in Unit 14. In *Det vore bra om…* it simply means "it would be good if…", and the verb after *om* goes into the past: *om du kom*, *om du kunde*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Feedback över en kanelbulle
dialogs.intro: The next day, at the three o'clock fika. Dian presented the sketches to the client yesterday. Karin sits down next to her with a cup of coffee.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Har du en minut? Jag tänkte ge dig lite feedback på presentationen i går.
lines.id: Have you got a minute? I wanted to give you some feedback on yesterday's presentation.
lines.literal: have you a minute? I thought give you little feedback on presentation-the yesterday.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Javisst. Var det så dåligt?
lines.id: Of course. Was it that bad?
lines.literal: yes-certainly. was it so bad?

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Tvärtom! Kunden var imponerad. Strukturen var tydlig och du höll tiden.
lines.id: Quite the opposite! The client was impressed. The structure was clear and you kept to time.
lines.literal: crosswise! customer-the was impressed. structure-the was clear and you held time-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vad skönt att höra. Fanns det något jag kunde ha gjort bättre?
lines.id: What a relief to hear. Was there anything I could have done better?
lines.literal: what nice to hear. was-there something I could have done better?

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Kanske en sak. Du sa ”förlåt” väldigt många gånger. Det behövs inte.
lines.id: Maybe one thing. You said "sorry" a great many times. There's no need.
lines.literal: maybe one thing. you said sorry very many times. it is-needed not.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Hemma är det artigt att vara ödmjuk. Här vet jag inte riktigt var gränsen går.
lines.id: Back home it's polite to be humble. Here I don't really know where the line is.
lines.literal: home is it polite to be humble. here know I not really where border-the goes.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Lagom är nyckeln. Inte för mycket och inte för lite, varken skryt eller ursäkter.
lines.id: Lagom is the key. Not too much and not too little: neither bragging nor apologies.
lines.literal: lagom is key-the. not too much and not too little, neither bragging nor excuses.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Lagom… Det är nog det svåraste ordet i hela svenskan.
lines.id: Lagom… That's probably the hardest word in the whole Swedish language.
lines.literal: lagom… that is probably the hardest word-the in whole Swedish-the.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Kanske det. En sak till: du skriver ”Bästa Karin” i dina mejl. ”Hej Karin” räcker gott.
lines.id: Maybe so. One more thing: you write "Dear Karin" in your emails. "Hi Karin" is plenty.
lines.literal: maybe that. one thing more: you write best Karin in your emails. hi Karin suffices well.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Och ”Med vänliga hälsningar” på slutet?
lines.id: And "Kind regards" at the end?
lines.literal: and with friendly greetings at end-the?

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Det passar bra till kunder. Till oss räcker ”Hälsningar” eller bara ditt namn.
lines.id: That's fine for clients. For us, "Regards" or just your name is enough.
lines.literal: that fits well to customers. to us suffices greetings or just your name.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Och vd:n? Ska jag säga ni till henne?
lines.id: And the CEO? Should I say *ni* to her?
lines.literal: and CEO-the? shall I say ni to her?

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Nej då, här säger alla du till alla. Så har det varit sedan sextiotalet.
lines.id: Oh no, everybody says *du* to everybody here. It's been that way since the sixties.
lines.literal: no then, here say all du to all. so has it been since sixties-the.

notes: **Jag tänkte ge dig lite feedback** — the past *tänkte* (thought) softens an announcement, just like English "I was thinking I'd…". Swedes say *feedback* in speech; in formal writing you will also see *återkoppling*. Note the reassuring order: positive first (*Tvärtom!*), then *kanske en sak*.
**Tvärtom** — "on the contrary, quite the opposite", stressed at the end: **tveh-TOM**. *Hålla tiden* (literally "hold the time") means to keep to the schedule, a quality Swedes value highly.

**Fanns det något jag kunde ha gjort bättre?** — modal + perfect from Unit 5: *kunde ha gjort* = could have done. Asking this question is a strong move in a Swedish workplace: it shows you take feedback seriously without being defensive.
**Var gränsen går** — literally "where the border goes": where the line is drawn. *En gräns* is also a national border: *gränsen mellan Sverige och Norge*.

**Lagom** — not too much, not too little; enough, just right. *Lagom varm* (pleasantly warm), *lagom stor* (the right size). There is a popular story that it comes from Vikings passing a drinking horn *laget om* (around the team), but linguists say it simply comes from an old word for "law, what is right". Say **LAH-gom**.

**Du till alla** — the *du-reformen* of the late 1960s swept away titles and the polite *ni*. Today Swedes say *du* to bosses, doctors, professors and the CEO (*vd:n*, **veh-DEH-en**, from *verkställande direktör*). Using *ni* to one person can sound old-fashioned or even distant, though some shops and restaurants use it to be extra polite.

grammars.title: The email ladder: openings and closings
body: Swedish emails are shorter and less ceremonial than English ones. Even a letter to an authority usually opens with *Hej*. Pick the rung that matches the reader.
after: **Bästa** + name is correct and polite, but slightly formal: fine for a first contact, a bit stiff between teammates. **Kära** (dear) is reserved for family and friends; never use it in a work email.
**Mvh** is short for *med vänlig hälsning* or *med vänliga hälsningar*; both forms are correct. Write your name on its own line after the closing, with no comma after the closing phrase.

sections.title: The unwritten rules: fika, lagom and consensus

blocks.text: **Fika** is not a coffee break you are free to skip. In most Swedish workplaces there is a morning and an afternoon *fika*, and the whole team sits down together, boss included. This is where news is shared, where newcomers are welcomed and, quite often, where decisions are quietly prepared before the meeting. Skipping it every day sends a signal you probably don't intend.

**Lagom** shapes behavior at work too: don't oversell yourself, don't apologize too much, don't work late every night to impress. Hierarchies are flat, everyone uses first names, and a manager who decides alone without asking the team is seen as a weak manager, not a strong one.

items: **Be on time.** Five minutes late to a meeting is late; a Swedish meeting starts and ends when the calendar says.
**Anchor before you decide** (*förankra*). Talk to the people concerned before the meeting, so nobody is surprised.
**Respect free time.** Calls and messages after five o'clock or during vacation are for emergencies only.
**July is closed.** Most Swedes take three or four weeks of *semester* in summer, and very little gets decided then.
**Feedback is mutual.** You are expected to give your manager feedback too, for example in the yearly *utvecklingssamtal* (development review).

blocks.title: Words for the meeting room
items: **en dagordning** — an agenda · **en punkt** — an item
**ett protokoll** — the minutes · **övriga frågor** — any other business
**att stämma av** — to check in, to touch base · **en avstämning** — a check-in meeting
**att förankra** — to anchor, to get buy-in · **ett beslut** — a decision

blocks.text: Here is the summary Dian sends the client after the meeting. It is short, friendly and to the point, which is exactly what a Swedish reader expects.

blocks.title: Ämne: Sammanfattning av mötet
items: Hej Anna,
Tack för ett bra möte i går. Som vi kom överens om skickar jag här en kort sammanfattning.
Vi börjar med bokningsfunktionen och räknar med att ha en första version klar den 15 maj. Inloggningen gör vi enkel i början.
Hör gärna av dig om du har frågor.
Vänliga hälsningar
Dian, praktikant i UX-teamet
**Ämne** — the subject line. Keep it short and concrete.
**Som vi kom överens om** — "as we agreed". The *som*-clause comes first, so the main verb *skickar* follows directly (V2).
**Räknar med att** — "expect to, count on". A safe, neutral way to promise a date.
**Hör gärna av dig** — "feel free to get in touch". *Gärna* turns an instruction into a friendly invitation.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 5
items: Feedback often looks backward. Say five sentences with modal + perfect about a project of your own: *Jag borde ha frågat tidigare.* *Vi kunde ha börjat med bokningen.* *Det hade varit bättre att…*
Then soften them with *kanske*: *Vi kunde kanske ha börjat med bokningen.*
